full_judgment:
3. The petitioner contested the case by filing written statement contending that the Complaint Case was not maintainable in law and on facts. The case of the petitioner was that the Complaint Case was not only barred by limitation but it was infructuous as the respondent No. 2 was dismissed from service on 24.6.1981. The petitioner contended that the respondent No. 2 was suspended for mis-appropriation of 15 tons of MS Rods. Respondent No. 2 was entrusted to take delivery of the said quantity of MS Rods from M/s. New Era Steel Engineering, Chittagong for sending to Dhaka through M/s. Rashid Enterprise, a carrying contractor of the Company. The respondent No. 2 although took delivery of the same he did not report about the missing of the same to the petitioner in due time. Charges were also framed against him on February 24.1979 to which respondent No. 2 duly submitted explanation but the explanation was not found satisfactorily by the petitioner and an Enquiry Committee was constituted. Before the said Committee the respondent No. 2 duly appeared. The Enquiry Committee after hearing the respondent No. 2 and examining the relevant materials placed before it submitted its report and on the basis of the report the petitioner dismissed the respondent No. 2 by an order dated 24.6.1981. The Labour Court fixed 26.6.1981 for ex-parte hearing of the case but on that date the petitioner filed an application to vacate the order for ex-parte hearing and also filed a written statement. On contest the Labour Court vacated the order of ex-parte hearing and fixed the date for peremptory hearing of the case on 14.7.1980. On that date the case was not heard. Thereafter respondent No. 2 filed an additional written statement on August 25, 1981. The petitioner filed a written objection praying for its rejection on the ground that as the same gave rise to a new cause of action it was barred by limitation. But the court accepted the additional written statement filed by the respondent No. 2. 

 6. Mr. Syed Amirul Islam first, contends that the Complaint Case No. 113 of 1981 was not maintainable as the respondent No. 2 filed grievance petition beyond the period of 15 days from the date of suspension on October 19, 1978 and on May 28, 1980. He secondly, submits that the additional written statement having given rise to a new cause of action and being filed after the period of limitation the Labour Court illegally relied upon the same and as such the judgment and order of the Court is vitiated. Thirdly, he submits that the Complaint Case No. 113 of 1981 was also barred by limitation. His next contention is that the Labour Court acted without jurisdiction in that it based its finding merely on the basis of the statement made in the Complaint petition without examining the respondent No. 2. His last contention is that the Labour Court itself although found that the domestic tribunal committed no defect in the procedure in holding the inquiry yet it came to the conclusion that the finding and decision of the Enquiry Committee was not fair and proper upon discussion of evidence already considered by the Domestic Tribunal and thereby arrived at its own independent finding without jurisdiction. The learned Counsel in aid of this submission cites decisions in the case of SH Quddus and others Vs. Chairman, Labour Court, Chittagong and others, 33 DLR 1, Manager, Zeal Bangla Sugar Mills Vs. Chairman, First Labour Court and another, 34 DLR 1, Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Vs. Chairman, Second Labour Court, Dacca and others.32 DLR 265 and the case of Md. Abdun Noor Vs. Platinum Jute Mills Ltd. and another, BSCR Vol. Nos.l and 2, page 467 to which we shall refer shortly. 

 Mr. Golam Rabbani vehemently canvassed that as the order of suspension and the order of dismissal were not supplied to the respondent No. 2 in violation of sub-section (4)(c) and sub-section (5) of section 18 of Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 the Labour Court rightly found that the finding and decision of the Domestic Tribunal were not fair and proper. He further, placing reliance upon section 25 of the Act, submits that the grievance with regard to subsistence allowance being a recurring one the grievance petition for payment of subsistence allowance was within time as the same can be filed on any date after the order of suspension was made and the rule of 15 days period does not apply to an order of suspension. Section 25 provides that any individual worker who has a grievance in respect of any matter covered under this Act shall bring his grievance to the notice of his employer, in writing, within 15 days of the occurrence of the cases of such grievance and if the employer fails to give a decision on the grievance petition within 15 days of the receipt of the grievance, he may make the complaint to the Labour Court within 30 days from the last date under clause (a) or within 30 days from the date of the decision. Mr. Rabbani submits that right to receive the subsistence allowance is a matter covered under this Act and as the same gives rise to a recurring cause of grievance the petition of grievance filed by the respondent No. 2 to the employer beyond the 15 days from the date of the order of suspension was within time. Section 25 of the Act, seems to us, provides that the grievance has to be brought to the notice of the employer in writing within 15 days of the occurrence of the cause of such grievance. In our opinion use of the definite article "the" before the expression "occurrence of the cause of such grievance" refers to original order by which a worker is aggrieved. In this case, the respondent No. 2 did not file the grievance petition for payment of subsistence allowance within 15 days of the date of the order of suspension made on 27.7.1978. He submitted it on 19.10.1978. The cause of grievance may be a recurring one as argued by the Respondent No. 2 but he is required to bring the grievance to the notice of the employer within 15 days of the order of suspension. Section 25 does not contemplate filing of a grievance notice after expiry of 15 days of the date of the order of suspension which gives rise to a cause of action. It does not speak that in case of an order of suspension the grievance notice may be filed after 15 days on the plea that cause of action in case of suspension is a recurring one. The cause of grievance refers to the order which gives rise to the cause of action. In this case there is no scope for us to read in section 25 of the Act any order other than the order of suspension and to put the construction as contended by the respondent No. 2 will lead to an absurd interpretation. Mr. Rabbani could not place before us any decision in support of this contention. In this case the grievance notice not having been filed within the statutory period of 15 days as contemplated in section 25 of the Act the Complaint Case No. 44 of 1981 before the Labour Court is not maintainable on the ground of limitation. 

 8. Now we shall proceed to see whether complaint petition No. 113 of 1981 is also barred by limitation. Mr. Rabbani places before us clause (c) of sub-section (4) of section 18 of the said Act to argue that the order inflicting punishment must be supplied to the worker concerned. Sub-section (5) of section 18 is as follows: 

 9. Relying upon this provision of law he canvassed that mere sending the order by registered post alone is not sufficient unless the employer satisfies about exhibition of the order on the notice board. He contends that the order complained of was not exhibited on the notice board. The mandate of sub-section (5) of section 18 of the Act is that in case of refusal by a worker to accept the order giving rise to a cause of grievance the employer must not only send the order to the address of the worker available from the record of the employer office but as well he must exhibit such document on the notice board of the employer office. If either of these two requirements is not satisfied there is no service of notice, order etc. such as contemplated in section 18 (4)(c) of the Act. Mr. Amirul Islam drawing our attention to Ext. 'Cha' repelled the contention of Mr. Rabbani by saying that the order was also exhibited on the notice board. He refers us to Ext. 'cha,' From Ext 'Cha' we fmd that the order was duly exhibited on the notice board. Therefore, the contention of Mr. Golam Rabbani is unfounded. Thus, the order of dismissal sent through registered post is treated as valid supply to the respondent No. 2 within the meaning of section 18(4)(c) of the Act as the same was exhibited on the notice board and sent through the registered post with acknowledgement receipt on refusal to accept the same by the respondent No.2. Accordingly, we hold that Labour Case No. 113 of 1981 having been filed after the expiry of the period on limitation as contemplated under section 25 is also barred by limitation. 

 11. Mr. Islam cites the decision in the case of Management Board, AR Howlader Jute Mills Ltd. Vs. Chairman of the First Labour Court, 28 DLR 368 to contend that in this case the additional written statement filed after expiry of the period of limitation prescribed for filing the complaint case gave rise to a new cause of action different from the cause of action stated in initial petition of complaint and the Labour Court illegally relied upon the same to arrive at its decision. He submits that in the instant case in amended paragraph No. 18(A) of the complaint petition the respondent No. 2 introduced a new cause of action regarding the defect of the Domestic Tribunal. On a reference to the judgment we find that the Labour Court relied upon paragraph No. 18(A) of the complaint petition to hold that the tribunal's decision was not fair and proper. As by the statement of paragraph No. 18(A) a new cause of grievance was introduced after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed in section 25 of the Act we hold that the Labour Court acted in excess of its jurisdiction in relying upon the additional written statement filed beyond period of limitation giving rise to new cause of action. We are of the opinion that on this ground judgment and order of the Labour Court is also liable to be struck down.
